One of the terms that is debated is the word "empire" and its meaning. As you read through the introduction to Ancient Empires, which definition do you agree with? Why do you agree with it? The Late Republic
⍞ Materials: Ancient Empires

➜ INTRO
Rome was founded in 753 BC, and it became a Republic in 509 BC. The Roman Republic had been involved in many wars. The most famous of these wars are known as the three Punic Wars. The Third Punic War was fought around 149-146 BC. During the Third Punic War, Rome would clash with a sovereign territory known as Carthage and ultimately would raze it to the ground. Rome would kill most of its male inhabitants and sell its women and children into slavery. With the defeat of Carthage, it would seem that Roman power was complete, as no other nation could stand in the way of its expansion.

However, the Roman Republic had internal issues. Its political and military leaders were corrupt, and despite its incredible growth, the Republic found itself in trouble. These political and military leaders were grasping for more power afforded them by their Republic governmental system. There were also internal struggles from people groups who refused to adapt to life under their new conquerors.

Learning from Plato and Aristotle
⍞ Materials: Christians Reading Classics

These two men have influenced both ancient world thinking and modern-day thinking about truth, virtue, the beginning of life, and other subjects. The apostles, early church fathers and mothers, and later Christian writers would all contend with Platonic and Aristotelian thought in their writings. As you read through this chapter, think about the amount of influence these two men had and why it's so important for Christians to read their works.

Introduction to Early Church Writings and Clement
⍞ Materials: Early Christian Writings
 
➜ INTRO
Imagine uncovering the writing of an Early Church Father as you sift through a monastic library in the East, or as you begin to use that writing as a wrapping paper for raw fish and seafood. That is the reality of some of these texts translated in this collection of Early Christian Writers.
These texts offer the modern-day reader more than early church doctrine and theology; they also offer us insights into the issues that the early church was facing as it began to follow the teachings of Christ.

➜ NOTE
The first- and second-century Christians are operating in a world wholly different than our own. They are operating in empires that have different values, virtues, and myths. Moreover, these people are trying to figure out Jesus, his relationship to God, and the connection of the Holy Spirit; and they are operating with the Septuagint (The Greek Translation of the Hebrew Bible), the Gospels, and some of the letters. Keep in mind that the canon of the Bible will not be official until the late fourth century.

As you read through these texts, take a moment to put your modern-day theological and biblical knowledge to the side. Listen to the words of these Christians. What are they asking? What are they teaching? Why might these be the questions that they are taking the time to answer? All of these questions can help us understand the early church world better and see where these early church writers are taking inspiration from.

➜ INTRO
There are many ways to measure the success of an emperor. One way is to measure the size of the nation that they ruled. It was under Emperor Trajan's rule that the Roman Empire reached its pinnacle in terms of territory.

Ignatius would write a series of letters to cities under his leadership, guiding them with doctrinal and practical practices that would help them live out their Christian faith.
